alt: Three steps in order: identify which Article 8.1 interest is affected, show an interference or a failure in a positive obligation, then move to Article 8.2. A note explains that the right is to respect for private and family life, which gives states room and grounds positive obligations; Article 8 is qualified.
caption: Interest, interference, then justification under 8.2.

alt: Article 8.1 at the centre with four interests: private life, with no exhaustive definition; family life, a question of fact based on real and close ties; home, where a person lives, protected against searches and serious environmental nuisance; and correspondence, covering letters, calls, emails and other communications.
caption: Name the interest before arguing interference.

alt: A table of seven strands of private life with their cases: integrity (X and Y v Netherlands), sexual life (Dudgeon v UK), identity (Goodwin v UK, leading to the Gender Recognition Act 2004), personal data (S and Marper v UK, leading to the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012), image (Peck v UK, Von Hannover v Germany), medical information (Campbell v MGN) and ending one’s life (Pretty v UK, Purdy).
caption: Private life is wide: body, identity, data, image, health and end-of-life choices.

alt: Marckx v Belgium: family life between an unmarried mother and child, with a breach of Article 8 with Article 14. Below, two home cases: López Ostra v Spain, fumes from a waste plant breached Article 8; Hatton v UK, the Heathrow night-flight scheme did not, because the state struck a fair balance with a wide margin.
caption: Family life depends on real ties; nuisance can breach the home, but the margin is wide.

alt: A timeline. 1975 Golder v UK: stopping a prisoner writing to a solicitor breached Article 8. 1984 Malone v UK: police phone tapping had no clear legal basis. 1985: the Interception of Communications Act followed. 1997 Halford v UK: interception of a senior officer’s office calls breached Article 8 because the 1985 Act did not regulate internal networks.
caption: Interference with communications needs a clear legal basis.

alt: Two routes take Article 8 into private disputes: positive obligations on the state, and the court as a public authority under section 6 HRA. Then a flow: Wainwright found no general privacy tort; Campbell developed misuse of private information; the test asks whether there is a reasonable expectation of privacy and whether it is outweighed by Article 10; Vidal-Hall confirmed it is a tort in its own right.
caption: Reasonable expectation of privacy first, then the balance against Article 10.

alt: Tom’s case in four steps: the photographs engage private life and the camera engages private life and home; the website is not a public authority but the court is, so Tom sues for misuse of private information; an addiction support group gives a strong expectation of privacy, as in Campbell; then balance against Article 10 and apply 8.2 to the camera.
caption: Argue the first stage fully, with authority, before moving to 8.2.
